subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Attention Economy: Your Eyes Are the Product
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Attention Economy: Your Eyes Are the Product usable.

hook.text: You're not Facebook's customer. You're its product. Advertisers are the customers. Your attention is what's being sold.

buildup.text: The attention economy: in a world of infinite content, human attention is the scarce resource everyone competes for.

discovery.text: Herbert Simon predicted it in 1971: 'A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.'

twist.text: Outrage, fear, and novelty capture attention best. So platforms optimize for them — not truth, not depth, not nuance.

climax.text: Every headline, notification, and autoplay video is engineered to steal seconds of your finite attention span.

punchline.text: If you're not paying for it, you're the product.

quiz.question: What is the 'attention economy'?
options: A system where human attention is the scarce resource being monetized

details.summary: In the attention economy, platforms compete for your time and engagement. Content is optimized not for truth or value but for the neurological responses that keep you scrolling, clicking, and returning.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding that your attention is the product being sold changes how you evaluate the information platforms serve you — it is not selected for your benefit.
takeaways: Platforms monetize attention through advertising and data
Content is algorithmically optimized for engagement, not truth
Awareness of the attention economy is a prerequisite for media literacy

faq.question: How do attention economy incentives distort the information you receive?
faq.answer: Algorithms promote content that generates emotional reactions — outrage, fear, surprise — because those emotions increase engagement. This systematically amplifies sensational, divisive, and emotionally manipulative content over calm, accurate reporting.

faq.question: What practical steps can you take to protect your attention from exploitation?
faq.answer: Turn off notifications, set time limits for social media, use RSS feeds or curated newsletters instead of algorithmic feeds, and recognize when content triggers strong emotions. Emotional intensity often signals algorithmic optimization rather than importance.
